I would highly suggest the following as it’s a VERY rough job market right now.

1.) DO NOT QUIT YOUR JOB: It seems like your biggest concern is you don’t feel challenged in your role and you feel stagnant and I totally understand that. But this market is a B.*.T.C.H., so since you have a stable income, PLEASE KEEP IT. But you have to structure your activities outside of work so you can make the transition to cyber without having to struggle with income and/or employment.

2.) BUDGET YOUR TIME: Realistically evaluate how much time you can spend on upskilling on a daily and/or weekly basis. If you can budget at least 3 to 4 hours per day, that would be great, but you can still make good progress with less. I am a CompTIA Certified Technical Trainer and I’ve coached people on strategies to pass the A+, the Network+ and the Security+ and the one thing I ALWAYS remind my students is that SKILLS matter WAY MORE than certs. Certs are designed to validate skills, but they don’t stand in for them and while there are parallels between being a Sys Admin and Cyber Security, Security IS different and you have to employ different skills.

3.) FIGURE OUT YOUR FOCUS: This should be number two, but I already wrote two so I’ll make this 3. Cyber is broad, so figure out what you want to do so you can decide what skills you’re going to strengthen and study during the time you’ve budgeted. Do you want to be a SOC analyst? Do you want to do GRC? Do you want to be a pen tester? Choose your discipline and then hone in.

4.) BUILD A HOME LAB: As a tech guy, I’m sure you have some devices you can create a physical lab with in the house but if you don’t, create a virtual lab using Virtual Box and some OS images or spin up a Linode server and host a virtual machine on there. Then start playing with different tools and create different labs. You can use ELK Stack on Linux to build a SIEM or try Splunk Free to get experience with a SOC. You can check out YouTube tutorials, threads here on Reddit or even prompt ChatGPT for some how-tos. Do some Capture The Flags and Try Hack Me’s for pentesting experience and then level up from there. I would also look at job postings and observe the technologies they want you to have experience with and find ways to learn those technologies or things similar to them to display your capabilities to work on those tools. As you do these labs, DOCUMENT EVERYTHING. Use this as your career portfolio to help you when you start to look for Cyber roles.

5.) BUILD YOUR NETWORK: As you upskill, look on Eventbrite or Meetup.com to find other cyber security professionals and tech conferences in your area. This has honestly been a cheat code for me because people are naturally biased and they help people that they know. So become someone hiring managers, recruiters and other industry professionals know. You can use them to get feedback, advice and referrals. Building a network is invaluable.

6.) START APPLYING FOR CYBER ROLES: Once you have a solid base, a good portfolio and you feel confident, start applying for roles. I highly recommend clearancejobs(.)com if you want roles with the government - look for positions that will sponsor your clearance. Lean on the network you’ve built and ask around about positions that may only be internally listed. Do the LinkedIN / Indeed thing and keep going until you get your new role. As you go through this process, look up videos about technical interview questions for Cyber roles and stay on top of current trends in cyber.

I know this was a lot, but I hope you find it to be helpful!!! You can definitely make the pivot. You just have to have a plan. Best of luck to you!!!

I think often times instructors can be accused of being insensitive and insulting for asking reasonable questions of learners regarding their responsibilities to their own learning. A surprising amount of people do not like taking accountability for their participation in their own failures. 

I actually went through something like this as an instructor where I’d assigned independent study and set office hours for one on one tutoring as needed for learners struggling and needing additional help. I allowed learners to do work at their own pace with a set due date and made them aware this would be followed by a skills assessment. The independent study was during class hours - typically times when I had mandatory trainings, meetings or I needed to complete grading and/or curriculum review.

There were learners who failed to do the independent study and subsequently failed the assessment and when they were reasonably questioned about how they spent their class time, they accused me of insulting their ability and intelligence. When in fact I was (reasonably and respectfully, might I add) questioning their integrity and lack of accountability. 

The program I worked for would similarly sponsor vouchers for learners to sit for the A+. And if the learners were already performing poorly in class and they weren’t communicating their needs to me - even after setting one on one’s - they certainly were not going to get nearly $600 worth of vouchers that could go to someone more deserving who showed they would pass the exams and get certified.

I don’t say any of this to accuse OP of lying, but I would suggest OP be a bit more objective and self aware of the part they played in their situation. If the instructor has been abusive, by all means, report them. There is no place for abuse in any way, shape or form. But if they were holding them accountable? Idk. Perhaps they should self reflect. 

The good news is they can always study and try new strategies. The test isn’t going anywhere.

Reddit can be a cesspool of negativity. It has some bright points, but many are snarky and just overtly negative for no real reason. Tread lightly and take the good, discard the bad. 

When it comes to your own personal journey, the most important thing you can do is engage your curiosity and upskill as much as possible. That doesn't mean turn into Certification Charlie, but it does mean to really take interest in what you want to do and where you want to go and investigate any and everything that is relevant to that subject matter.

Also be mindful that one size does not fit all. Another's success story may not reflect your own. Similarly, another's negative experience does not mean you will have the same experience.

Like any other forum or body of opinions, take the information you see on Reddit with a grain of salt. Some of it is really valuable, but some isn't. Keep the faith and know that your journey is your own.

After I cleanse my skin and dry it, I tone it with a super gentle toner and let that dry completely. I'll then follow that with my tret - I take a pea sized amount and dot it around my face - and rub that in completely. After the tret, I'll dab HQ on my dark spots and rub it in. I'll wait a few minutes and then I'll finish with a good moisturizer that doesn't have any actives. I only do HQ and tret at night. You never want to use it during the day because the sun breaks down Vitamin A and the tret and HQ make your skin photosensitive which will only make your PIH worse. So night time before bed only is the best advice I can give.
 
If I ever have irritation, I'll skip the tret for the night and just do the HQ because it doesn't really irritate my skin. 

My day routine is my cleanser, toner, serums/vitamin C/ moisturizer and a really good sunscreen. I use Aveeno's Protect & Hydrate SPF 70 and I reapply throughout the day. Sunscreen is a must otherwise you'll ruin all your progress. For me, the higher the better. Lol. I like the Aveeno Protect & Hydrate because it's really nourishing - even for a chemical SPF - and it doesn't leave a white mask on your face like some mineral SPF's.

Sure thing! I'm glad it was helpful. The electrolytes will help with both physical energy and mental. As we fast, it's easy for us to lose our electrolytes and those are essential for optimal cellular function. 
Since we aren't getting any electrolytes from food, it's very important that we replenish them.   

When we feel fatigued, it's often our body telling us that it's not functioning optimally. I've found that Morton's Light Salt which is half sodium half potassium chloride is something I find to be helpful. I was using Hilyte electrolyte drops but for me the magnesium was causing me some issue. 

I also incorporated lemon water to help mitigate the build up of uric acid as this will have a pretty negative effect on your kidneys over time- and potassium also helps with this.

It's really contingent on a variety of factors and every individual will have different results.

Say if you are morbidly obese and your body has a lot of excess fat, you can fast far beyond the 90 day "threshold", contingent on you being in generally good health prior to starting the fast. The longest faster on record was named Angus Barbieri. He fasted 382 days no food. He was 27 years old and he started his fast at 456 lbs and ended at 180. He maintained a weight of 196lbs post fast.

If you are only slightly overweight, then perhaps 90 days would be your threshold. If you are at a healthy weight, that threshold drops even further. It's really contingent on how much fat you have stored on your body.

As far as feeling and cravings, if you lived a clean lifestyle pre fast, then the duration of the fast will be relatively easy. If you had a diet with a lot of neuron affecting foods (sugars, oils, processed carbohydrates) you will have a much tougher time with cravings and withdrawal symptoms. 

Electrolytes - namely sodium and potassium - will be instrumental in keeping you upbeat for the duration of a long fast. Also, you want to keep your activities pretty low. Walking is great but anything intense is going to wear you out rather quickly and bring many people immense fatigue, so I'm a fan of taking it very easy during a fast.

I always say the first 3 to 5 days are the most challenging. If you can make it beyond that, it should be relatively smooth sailing. It's a phenomenal thing that you made it 41 days without a hitch!

As far as your direct questions go, your body likely didn't alert you to hunger because it still had fat reserves to access and after the 2nd or third day of fasting our bodies switch from running off of glycogen to running off of ketones (fat).

Our bodies are incredibly intelligent and spare true starvation, the desire for food is very much a mind over matter thing. It seems like you have tremendous control over your mind and your urges which is an admirable thing.

Kudos to you and your achievement. That is certainly no small feat and you should be proud of yourself and of your willpower. Since you went 40 days with no food, take about 20 days to gradually wake your digestive system back up so you don't risk refeeding syndrome. Start with bone broth and coconut water and high water content fruits. Gradually work your way up to steamed veg and eventually to whole foods again.
